title: Hosted API Demo - Chat/Text Generation Basics
summary: Introductory hosted API demo focused on chat and text generation basics: streaming, key params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retries and backoff, SDK examples. Discussed security briefly (SOC2, KMS), cost/latency tradeoffs, and next steps: send pricing, security pack, and schedule PoC perf benchmark with sample prompts.
topics: Generation parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
next_steps: Redwood to send hosted pricing sheet and sample SLA (Maya)
SE to share security whitepaper and SOC2 report (Diego)
Customer to provide representative prompt set for benchmark (Ben)
Schedule 1-hr PoC perf run next week (tentative: 2026-03-26)
Follow-up meeting to review PoC results and pilot scope
action_items: Maya: Send pricing + quickstart links by 2026-03-20
Diego: Share security docs + integration guide by 2026-03-21
Ben: Upload prompt set and expected QPS by 2026-03-22
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya with Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on this account. Diego from our SE team will run the demo. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Aisha Khan: Hi Aisha here, CTO at Peregrine.
[00:10] Ben Porter: Ben, lead ML.
[00:12] Lydia Park: Lydia, product.
[00:13] Tom: Tom, SRE.
[00:16] Diego Alvarez: Diego here, thanks all. We'll go through hosted API basics for chat/text gen, streaming, key params and some retry best practices.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Timeline wise we'll be ~40 minutes, then open Q&A. If we hit enterprise security stuff we'll flag it for Diego to send more detail.
[00:35] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. We're mainly evaluating hosted first; timeline is end of Q2 for a pilot, key constraints are latency under 300ms p50 for short responses and strict data residency/SOC2.
[00:49] Ben Porter: Also want to understand cost at scale — ~10k requests/day with typical 60 tokens output.
[00:55] Diego Alvarez: Great. I'll start with a live curl and SDK example then show streaming and retries. Note: demo uses a smaller prompt set to keep latency low.
[01:05] [01:05] Diego shares screen: Code sample in Node SDK.
[01:12] Diego Alvarez: Here's a simple chat call using Redwood hosted endpoints - you can see we set model: "redwood-2.1-chat", messages array, and a few params: temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 80, top_p: 0.95.
[01:24] Lydia Park: Quick Q — default temperature meaning?
[01:26] Diego Alvarez: Lower temperature means more deterministic output; 0.0 is very repeatable, 0.2 is usually good for assistant style. Higher yields more creative.
[01:33] Ben Porter: And top_p interacts with temp?
[01:35] Diego Alvarez: Yes they both shape randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling. Use one or tune both, we can recommend per workload.
[01:42] [01:42] Diego runs a curl example showing streaming via server-sent events (SSE).
[01:48] Diego Alvarez: Streaming returns tokens as they are generated — lower time-to-first-byte. In Node we pipe events; in Python you can iterate over the stream.
[01:58] Tom (SRE): Is streaming over WebSocket supported?
[02:01] Diego Alvarez: We offer SSE for REST and WebSocket for persistent connections; both supported. WebSocket is useful for high concurrency UIs.
[02:10] Aisha Khan: How do you handle partial failures while streaming?
[02:13] Diego Alvarez: We include event markers for end-of-stream and error events; clients should retry based on idempotency token. For long streaming sessions we recommend a heartbeat and resumable tokens — we surfaced those in our SDK.
[02:25] [02:25] Diego shows retry/backoff snippet.
[02:27] Diego Alvarez: For non-streaming calls we recommend exponential backoff with jitter. If a request is side-effect free (generation), you can safely retry with the same idempotency key. For stateful operations we advise checkpointing.
[02:40] Ben Porter: What about rate limits and throttling? We might have traffic bursts from product tests.
[02:44] Diego Alvarez: Hosted plan has per-account rate limits; we expose error 429 with Retry-After. For bursty workloads we recommend token bucket smoothing client-side or contact Redwood for burst capacity / Dedicated if sustained.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Worth noting Dedicated gives reserved capacity and predictable throughput if you need consistent latency at scale.
[03:05] Aisha Khan: We're trying to avoid Dedicated initially due to ops overhead but may consider later.
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: Totally, hosted often covers early pilots. Also we support prefix caching and KV cache for assistant scenarios to save on tokens and latency — transparent on the runtime side.
[03:21] Ben Porter: Can you explain KV cache vs prefix cache?
[03:24] Diego Alvarez: Prefix caching stores repeated prompt prefixes (like system messages or long context) while KV cache refers to the key/value attention cache used during decoding — we cache whole sequences for reuse to avoid recomputation on similar prompts. Both reduce cost and latency for assistant flows.
[03:39] [03:39] Diego runs a short local benchmark: single-threaded p50 latency for a 32 token generation.
[03:45] Diego Alvarez: In our internal test this model on hosted returns ~180ms p50 for small prompts — your mileage will vary by sequence length and model.
[03:52] Lydia Park: That's promising. For cost estimation, how do you report tokens and billing?
[03:56] Maya Chen: Billing is per input/output tokens; Console shows token-level breakdown per request. We also provide sample cost per 1M tokens in the pricing sheet.
[04:05] Aisha Khan: Security — SSO and KMS are must-haves. Any limitations on data retention?
[04:10] Diego Alvarez: Hosted defaults to 30-day retention for logs but you can opt-out; Enterprise/RBAC and SSO/SAML are supported. For encryption we integrate with customer KMS for key management in Private/Dedicated; hosted can be configured with customer-managed keys for specific plans. SOC 2 report available.
[04:26] Tom (SRE): Do you support VPC peering for Private control plane?
[04:29] Diego Alvarez: Yes VPC options and on-prem bundles available for large enterprise. We'll send the tech spec.
[04:35] [04:35] Diego switches back to code showing error handling.
[04:38] Diego Alvarez: Example: handle 429/503 with backoff, for 500 it's transient but if persistent we escalate. We also expose request IDs so you can correlate logs with our tracing.
[04:48] Ben Porter: Any SDKs for Go? Python/Node are fine but Go would be ideal for us.
[04:52] Diego Alvarez: We have official SDKs for Node, Python, and a community Go client; enterprise customers can get an official Go SDK roadmap.
[04:59] [05:00] Lydia Park: On prompt engineering: do you have tools to guard outputs or content filters?
[05:03] Diego Alvarez: Yes we provide safety filters and allow custom filters for enterprise; Console can flag out-of-policy outputs and you can route to human review.
[05:12] Maya Chen: Quick demo of the Console — Diego, can you show streaming traces and token cost breakdown?
[05:16] [05:16] Diego shares Console: traces view with per-request token counts and latency waterfall.
[05:23] Diego Alvarez: Here you see streaming chunks in the trace, cost per token, and routes by model. You can set per-model quotas and alerts on latency regressions.
[05:33] Aisha Khan: For our pilot we want automatic fallbacks if the main model is overloaded. Is that supported?
[05:37] Diego Alvarez: Yes Smart Routing can fail over to a compatible model variant (e.g., quantized variant) or a different region; you configure fallback policy per route.
[05:46] Ben Porter: Can fallbacks preserve response quality?
[05:48] Diego Alvarez: It'll differ; we recommend a canary rollout and run comparative evals — Redwood Optimize can help with model selection and quantization advice tied to your prompts.
[05:58] [05:58] Ben does a quick voice note: "We should run a 2-model comparison for our top-10 prompts."
[06:03] Diego Alvarez: Perfect — we can run PoC perf + quality comparison.
[06:08] Lydia Park: About retries again — if we stream and get a mid-stream disconnect, what's best practice to resume without duplicating content?
[06:14] Diego Alvarez: Use idempotency keys and sequence offsets. Our SDK supports stream resumptions with a small resume token; server will supply last acked token index. We'll include example code.
[06:26] Tom (SRE): Any abnormal costs from retries? If client retries aggressively during an outage we could blow tokens.
[06:31] Diego Alvarez: Right — recommend client-side de-dup and conservative retry policy; we also support rate-limit headers and quota alerts. For critical workloads you can enable request-cost ceilings.
[06:43] Maya Chen: I'll also note that Optimize suggests batching windows and quantization for cost savings on steady workloads.
[06:49] Aisha Khan: On data residency we need EU-only processing for a subset of traffic. Is region pinning available?
[06:54] Diego Alvarez: Yes you can route requests to region-specific endpoints and pin to EU models; Console shows region-level telemetry.
[07:02] [07:02] Diego runs a short example switching model param to lower max_tokens and showing cost drop.
[07:10] Diego Alvarez: Lowering max_tokens and using aggressive stop sequences can greatly reduce output tokens — big lever for cost. Also streaming reduces perceived latency which matters for UX.
[07:21] Ben Porter: Do you expose tokenization tooling so we can precompute token counts client-side?
[07:25] Diego Alvarez: We provide tokenizer libraries and tokenizers repo; you can estimate tokens before calling the API to enforce ceilings.
[07:34] Lydia Park: Anything else on observability?
[07:36] Diego Alvarez: We have tracing headers, per-request cost, latency breakdown, and integrated alerts. You can export telemetry to your observability stack.
[07:44] [07:44] Maya Chen: Ok going to quick recap and next steps — Maya: recap: send pricing, Diego: security docs + PoC run, Ben: provide prompt set.
[07:54] Aisha Khan: We want a perf run with 100 QPS synthetic and also a realistic run 10 RPS with bursts.
[08:02] Diego Alvarez: We'll scope that in the PoC plan. Estimated run likely 1–2 hours plus analysis.
[08:09] Ben Porter: If we do go to Dedicated later what's typical lead time?
[08:12] Maya Chen: Dedicated provisioning is typically 2–6 weeks depending on region and capacity. We'll share exact SLAs in the docs.
[08:21] Lydia Park: Any licensing or minimums for hosted enterprise?
[08:24] Maya Chen: There are usage tiers; enterprise plans have minimum monthly commitments for SLA-backed support — details in the pricing sheet.
[08:32] Tom (SRE): Security question — are logs searchable by customers only?
[08:36] Diego Alvarez: Yes, customer logs are isolated; audit logs, RBAC and SSO available. We'll include the architecture diagram.
[08:45] [08:45] Maya Chen: Alright we'll wrap. Thanks all — I'll send follow-ups and link to quickstart. Any final Qs?
[08:51] Aisha Khan: No more for now, thanks that's helpful.
[08:54] Ben Porter: Thanks.
[08:55] Lydia Park: Thanks everyone.
[08:56] Maya Chen: Great, next steps noted.
[08:58] [END]
